viewpoints.claim: A message about the result of an action, a wait, progress or errors that appears without moving focus is exposed to assistive tech as a status (role=status, role=alert or an aria-live region), so a screen reader announces it without the user losing their place.

source.author: W3C Accessibility Guidelines Working Group
source.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to make users aware of important changes in content that are not given focus, and to do so in a way that doesn't unnecessarily interrupt their work.

prefers: role="status" (polite) for results, saved and progress messages such as '18 results returned' or 'Saved'
role="alert" only for messages that must interrupt, such as an error that blocks the task
The live region rendered empty with the page and its text changed later, so the browser is already watching it
aria-busy="true" on a live region while it fills, then false, so half-loaded content is not read out
forbids: A 'Saved' or 'Added to basket' message painted as plain text with no live role
Moving focus to a success message just so it gets read, when the user was still working
Injecting the live region and its text in the same tick, which many screen readers do not announce
Every message as role=alert, so routine confirmations interrupt whatever is being read

measure.what: Walk every action that adds a message without navigating (save, add to basket, filter, copy, upload, inline submit). For each text node that appears within 3 s of the action and is not inside the focused element, count it when no ancestor has role=status|alert|log|progressbar or aria-live=polite|assertive, or when that live ancestor was itself inserted in the same mutation as the text. Count must be 0.
measure.mustFail:
Clicking 'Add to basket' inserts
Added to basket
beside the button; no role, no aria-live; focus stays on the button.
measure.mustPass:
The page loads with an empty
; clicking 'Add to basket' sets its text to 'Added to basket, 3 items'; focus stays on the button.

exceptions: Changes of context (a new page, a dialog that takes focus) are announced by focus and are outside this rule
New content itself (the list of search results) is not a status message; the line about it ('18 results') is
The 3 s window is uxcli's, not W3C's
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Any screen that confirms, filters or saves in place needs it; brochure and article pages often have no in-place messages at all.

viewpoints.claim: A finished transaction ends on a confirmation page whose panel states the outcome as a heading, gives the reference number if there is one, says what happens next and when, how to get in touch, and offers a way to keep a record.

source.author: GOV.UK Design System
source.quote: Confirmation pages reassure users that they have completed a transaction and helps them understand what to expect next.

prefers: A panel whose h1 says the outcome ('Application complete') with the reference number beneath it
A 'What happens next' section with a timescale ('We'll email you within 5 working days')
Contact details for the service, links to what users are likely to need next, and a save-as-PDF or print link
A page that still answers sensibly when it is revisited from a bookmark
forbids: A toast reading 'Submitted!' over the form the user just filled in
A thank-you page with no reference number for a transaction that has one
Links or buttons inside the green panel without changing its focus and contrast styles

measure.what: Complete the journey to its last page. Count missing items among: (a) an h1 that names the outcome (contains a past-tense verb or 'complete'/'confirmed'/'received'); (b) the reference number, when the back end issued one, as visible text; (c) a heading or paragraph about what happens next containing a time expression (a day, date or duration); (d) a contact method (mailto:, tel: or a contact link); (e) a print, download or email-me-a-copy control. Count must be 0.
measure.mustFail: After 'Pay now' the page shows a centred tick and 'Thank you!' with a 'Back to home' button; the order number exists in the API response but is not on the page.
measure.mustPass: The page shows a panel 'Order confirmed — your reference is HDJ2123F', a 'What happens next' section saying 'We'll send it by Friday 10 October', a phone number and 'Download a PDF receipt'.

exceptions: GOV.UK also asks for a link to a feedback page; that is a government service requirement, not counted here
A step that is part of a longer task, where the user has not finished, uses a success banner on the next page instead (GOV.UK notification banner)
The past-tense and time-expression heuristics are uxcli's
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Checkout and application journeys end in a transaction; a marketing sign-up or a workspace action that creates something may; reading and dashboards do not.

viewpoints.claim: A toast is only for a short, low-priority confirmation of something the user just did; an error that needs action, a warning, or anything the user cannot find again elsewhere goes in an inline message or banner that stays.

source.author: Shopify Polaris
source.quote: Avoid using toast for critical information that merchants need to act on immediately.

prefers: Short noun + verb confirmations: 'Product updated', 'Collection added'
Errors the user must fix shown next to the cause or in a banner that persists until resolved
Whatever the toast says also visible somewhere on the page after it goes (the saved value, the item in the list, a notifications area)
forbids: A validation or payment error delivered only as a toast that auto-dismisses
A toast that holds the only copy of a generated password, link or code
Several sentences of explanation in a toast

measure.what: Record a walk through every action, including forced failures (offline, 4xx, 5xx). Treat as a toast any fixed- or absolute-positioned element with role=status|alert or aria-live that is removed or hidden within 15 s without user input. Count toasts whose text matches error/failed/could not/denied/invalid, toasts with more than 15 words, and toasts whose distinctive text (any token of 6+ characters other than common words) appears nowhere in the DOM 2 s after they leave. Count must be 0.
measure.mustFail: Submitting a card that is declined shows a red toast 'Payment failed: your card was declined, try another card' for 4 s; the form shows nothing.
measure.mustPass: A declined card shows an error summary above the form and a message by the card field; a successful save shows the toast 'Settings saved' and the new values stay in the fields.

exceptions: Polaris allows an error toast for system errors not caused by the user, such as 'Internet disconnected', in 3 words
Polaris's own Toast component is deprecated in favour of the App Bridge Toast API; the guidance quoted is still on its page
The 15 s, 15-word and 6-character thresholds are uxcli's
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Toasts live in apps, shops and transactions; static marketing and content pages rarely show them.

viewpoints.claim: A toast that carries an action (Undo, Retry, View) stays at least 10 seconds or until dismissed, and the same action can be reached somewhere else on the page.

source.author: Shopify Polaris
source.quote: Toast with action should persist for at least 10,000 milliseconds to give the merchant enough time to act on it.

prefers: An actionable toast that persists until the user dismisses it (Carbon's rule)
One short verb as the action label: Undo, Retry, View
The same Undo or Retry reachable another way: a restore from trash, a reload, a history entry
Auto-dismiss timers paused while the toast is hovered or has focus inside it
forbids: An Undo toast that vanishes after 3–5 seconds
Undo offered only in the toast, with no trash, history or other way back
'OK', 'Got it' or 'Dismiss' as the toast's action

measure.what: Trigger each action that shows a toast. For each toast containing a button or link other than close, record how long it stays in the DOM and visible with no user input; count those under 10 000 ms. Then for each such action label, search the page (menus included) for another control with the same accessible name or a trash/history route; count toasts whose action has no second route. Count must be 0.
measure.mustFail: Deleting a file shows 'File deleted  [Undo]' that disappears after 4 s; there is no trash view.
measure.mustPass: Deleting a file shows 'File deleted  [Undo]' that stays until closed, and the file can also be restored from Trash.

exceptions: Carbon asks that actionable toasts persist until dismissed, which is stricter than Polaris's 10 seconds
A toast without an action may auto-dismiss (Polaris's default is 5000 ms) when its content is available elsewhere, which WCAG 2.2.1 lists as not needing to be adjustable
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Undo and Retry toasts belong to tools and shop admin; marketing pages do not offer them, and transaction flows usually confirm on a page.

viewpoints.claim: Choose the loading indicator by the wait: nothing under about a second, an indeterminate spinner or skeleton for one to three seconds, and a determinate progress bar with a label for longer operations whose progress is known, placed where the result will appear.

source.author: GitHub Primer
source.quote: Determinate loading indicators work best for processes that are likely to take longer (approximately 3 or more seconds).

prefers: No loading state under 1 s, so nothing flashes
A skeleton when the shape of the content is known; a spinner for a button action or a region whose shape is not
<progress> or role=progressbar with aria-valuenow for uploads, downloads, imports and exports of known size
A specific label: 'Loading status checks', 'Uploading 3 of 12 files', not just 'Loading'
The indicator in the region it stands in for; long jobs moved to the background so the page stays usable
forbids: A full-page overlay spinner when one panel is loading
An indeterminate spinner for a 40 s upload whose byte count is known
A spinner that appears and disappears in a few hundred milliseconds on every click
A static hourglass or 'Please wait' text with no motion and no progress

measure.what: Record the walk unthrottled and again with network throttled (Slow 3G). Count: (a) loading indicators (role=progressbar, aria-busy=true, elements matching spinner|loader|skeleton) visible for less than 1000 ms in the unthrottled run when the request itself took under 1000 ms; (b) uploads or downloads of a known byte size that run longer than 3 s throttled without an element exposing aria-valuenow or a <progress value>; (c) indicators whose bounding box covers more than 80% of the viewport while the request being waited on fills a region smaller than half the viewport; (d) indicators with no accessible name. Count must be 0.
measure.mustFail: Uploading a 20 MB file shows a centred full-screen spinner with no label for 45 s; every tab switch flashes the same overlay for 150 ms.
measure.mustPass: The upload shows '<progress value=42 max=100>' labelled 'Uploading report.pdf, 42%' in the file row while the rest of the page stays usable; tab switches under a second show no indicator.

exceptions: Primer's bands (under 1 s, 1–3 s, 3–10 s, over 10 s) are general guidance; it says waits cannot be predicted exactly
An interstitial loading page is acceptable for a long process that ends in a significant change, such as creating a repository
The 80% and half-viewport thresholds are uxcli's
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Apps, dashboards, shops and transactions wait on servers; static pages rarely show loading states.

viewpoints.claim: Animation durations come from a small set of tokens and grow with the size of the change: about 70–150 ms for button and toggle feedback, around 240 ms for a toast or expansion, 400 ms for large expansion, 700 ms only for background dimming.

source.author: IBM Carbon Design System
source.quote: Motion’s duration should be dynamic based on the size of the animation; the larger the change in distance (traveled) or size (scaling) of the element, the longer the animation takes.

prefers: Named duration tokens (duration-fast-01 70ms, duration-fast-02 110ms, duration-moderate-01 150ms, duration-moderate-02 240ms, duration-slow-01 400ms, duration-slow-02 700ms) instead of ad hoc values
Productive (faster, subtler) motion for task UI; expressive motion only for occasional significant moments
Ease-out on user input; micro-interactions within 90–120 ms per Carbon's checklist
Motion that answers a question: what changed, where it came from, that the action registered
forbids: A 600 ms transition on a button hover
The same long duration on a tooltip and on a full-screen panel
Decorative motion nobody asked for that is noticed on every use

measure.what: Read computed transition-duration and animation-duration (plus delay) on every element that changes on :hover, :focus, :active, [aria-expanded], [aria-checked] or [data-state], and on elements that enter or leave during the walk. Excluding loading indicators and media, count: animations longer than 700 ms; changes on buttons, links, checkboxes, switches and tabs longer than 150 ms; and pairs where a smaller element's duration exceeds that of a larger one (by bounding-box area) that changes in the same interaction. Count must be 0.
measure.mustFail: Buttons transition background over 500 ms, a toast slides in over 1200 ms, and a full-width drawer opens in 150 ms.
measure.mustPass: Buttons change in 110 ms, the toast enters in 240 ms, the drawer opens in 400 ms and its scrim fades in 700 ms.

exceptions: Carbon says dynamic, size-based duration is preferred and the six static tokens are an interim implementation; other systems have other scales
Expressive motion for a page change or an important moment may sit at the slow end
Grouping elements into 'micro-interaction' controls and comparing by bounding-box area are uxcli's operationalisation
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Every kind animates something; the scale is about proportion, not about the kind of page.

viewpoints.claim: Anything that starts moving, blinking or scrolling on its own and lasts more than five seconds, and anything that auto-updates (carousels, tickers, live feeds, background video), has a visible control to pause, stop or hide it.

source.author: W3C Accessibility Guidelines Working Group
source.work: Understanding Success Criterion 2.2.2: Pause, Stop, Hide (WCAG 2.2)
source.quote: Content that moves or auto-updates can be a barrier to anyone who has trouble reading stationary text quickly as well as anyone who has trouble tracking moving objects.

prefers: A labelled Pause/Play button on carousels, marquees, background video and animated hero illustrations
Auto-updating feeds with a pause or a way to choose the update frequency
Real-time data (stock ticker, auction timer) that jumps to the current state when resumed
No autoplay at all where the motion carries no information
forbids: An auto-advancing carousel whose only stop is hovering or focusing it
A looping background video with no control
A news ticker that scrolls forever

measure.what: Load each page and wait 6 s without input. Count elements still animating (running CSS animations or Web Animations with iteration count above 1 or infinite, <video autoplay> playing, a carousel whose visible slide changed, or a region whose text changed on a timer) that have no visible, keyboard-reachable control whose accessible name contains pause, stop, hide or turn off. Exclude loading indicators shown while a request is pending. Count must be 0.
measure.mustFail: A homepage hero carousel advances every 4 s and pauses only on hover; a muted background video loops with no controls.
measure.mustPass: The carousel has a 'Pause slideshow' button before the slides and the video has a 'Pause background video' button; both stop motion when pressed.

exceptions: Motion that is part of an activity where it is essential (a game, an animation preview) is exempt
Moving content that stops by itself within 5 seconds and runs in parallel with other content does not need a control; auto-updating content has no such 5-second exception
A pause that only holds while the pointer or focus is on the element does not count as a mechanism
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Carousels and background video are marketing, content and shop staples; live-updating dashboards and tools sometimes auto-update; transaction flows rarely move on their own.

viewpoints.claim: When a session or form times out, the user is warned before it happens and can extend it with a simple action, given at least 20 seconds to respond, or the limit can be turned off or lengthened.

source.author: W3C Accessibility Guidelines Working Group
source.quote: Providing options to disable time limits, customize the length of time limits, or request more time before a time limit occurs helps those users who require more time than expected to successfully complete tasks.

prefers: No time limit where none is needed
A warning dialog before expiry, announced and focused, with 'Stay signed in' as the primary action
At least 20 seconds to respond to the warning; extending possible at least ten times
After a time-out, the user's answers kept so they can continue once signed in again
forbids: Silent session expiry that discards a half-filled form
A timed redirect ('You will be taken to the home page in 5 seconds') with no way to stop it
A warning that appears only as a toast or banner outside the user's focus

measure.what: With the clock accelerated (or the session TTL shortened) on each authenticated or multi-step page, leave the page idle until the time limit. Count limits that expire with no prior warning; warnings that give less than 20 s between appearing and expiry; warnings with no keyboard-reachable control that extends the session; meta refresh or JavaScript redirects that fire on a timer with no control to stop them; and expiries after which previously entered field values are lost. Count must be 0.
measure.mustFail: After 15 idle minutes on step 3 of an application the next submit lands on the sign-in page and the answers on steps 1–3 are gone; no warning appeared.
measure.mustPass: At 13 minutes a dialog says 'You'll be signed out in 2 minutes' with a focused 'Stay signed in' button; pressing it resets the timer, and if ignored, signing back in returns to step 3 with answers kept.

exceptions: Real-time events such as auctions, and limits that are essential or longer than 20 hours, are exempt
Security limits such as one-time codes can be essential, but other criteria (redundant entry, accessible authentication) still apply
Answers being kept after a time-out comes from WCAG 2.2.5 Re-authenticating (AAA), referenced from this page, not from 2.2.1 itself
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Time limits come with sign-in and long forms: transactions and signed-in tools; checkout sessions and dashboards sometimes; public pages almost never.

viewpoints.claim: Every alert, banner and toast names its type in words — Success, Error, Warning, Information — as the first word or its heading, used the same way across the product, not only through its colour or icon.

source.author: U.S. Web Design System
source.quote: Users should be able to understand the purpose of the alert without relying solely on its color or the shape of its icon.

prefers: A heading such as 'Success', 'Error' or 'Warning' (GOV.UK uses 'Success' on its green notification banner)
The same heading word for the same type everywhere in the service
An icon per type with a text alternative, in addition to the word
The alert's ARIA role matched to its urgency (status for success, alert for errors)
forbids: A green box and a red box with otherwise identical wording styles
An icon-only type indicator with alt=""
'Success' in one place and 'Done!' or 'Yay' for the same type elsewhere

measure.what: Collect every alert, banner, toast and inline notification shown during the walk (role=alert|status, aria-live, or class/name matching alert|banner|toast|notification|callout). Count those whose heading or first five words of accessible text contain none of: success, successful, error, warning, important, information, info, notice, announcement, emergency, problem, failed, complete. Then count types (by colour family) that use more than one such word across the product. Count must be 0.
measure.mustFail: A save shows a green box reading 'Your changes are live'; a failure shows a red box reading 'Something went sideways' with a decorative icon whose alt is empty.
measure.mustPass: A save shows a banner headed 'Success' reading 'Your changes are live'; a failure shows one headed 'Error' with 'Error' as the icon's text alternative.

exceptions: USWDS allows the type word in the body rather than the lead when leading with it would make the alert unclear
The word list and the five-word window are uxcli's
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Wherever outcomes are reported back; marketing and content pages show alerts less often.

viewpoints.claim: An action that destroys the user's work never completes on a single click with no way back: it asks for confirmation in a dialog, or it completes and offers Undo with a route to restore.

source.author: U.S. Web Design System
source.work: Alert component — When to consider something else
source.quote: If an action will result in destroying a user’s work (for example, deleting an application) use a more intrusive pattern, such as a confirmation modal dialogue, to allow the user to confirm that this action is what they want.

prefers: Undo (in a persistent toast, a trash or a version history) for actions that can be reversed
A confirmation dialog for actions that cannot be reversed
Bulk and irreversible deletes behind a confirmation, single reversible deletes behind Undo
forbids: A trash icon that deletes immediately and permanently
Only an alert or toast announcing the deletion after the fact, with no Undo
A confirmation dialog for every trivial, reversible action, which teaches users to click through it

measure.what: Activate every control whose name or icon matches delete, remove, discard, clear, reset, archive, cancel subscription or close account on a disposable fixture. Count those where, within 2 s, the object is gone from the DOM (and from a reload) with no role=dialog|alertdialog having appeared and no visible control named Undo/Restore/Revert, and no trash, archive or history route that lists the object. Count must be 0.
measure.mustFail: Clicking the bin icon on a saved report removes the row and the report is gone after reload; no dialog, no Undo, no trash.
measure.mustPass: Clicking the bin icon removes the row and shows 'Report deleted  [Undo]' until dismissed, and the report sits in Trash for 30 days; 'Delete all' opens a dialog 'Delete 14 reports?'.

exceptions: Clearing transient input (a search box, a filter) is not destroying work
USWDS names the confirmation dialog; offering Undo instead for reversible actions follows Polaris's toast guidance and is this pool's reading, not USWDS's words
The 2 s window is uxcli's
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Tools that hold the user's work have destructive actions; shops have removable baskets and accounts; marketing and reading pages do not.
